formulaCard.title: Mean Formula

explanation: The [[kw:mean]] (or arithmetic average) is the sum of all values divided by the number of values.
Formula: $$\text{Mean} = \frac{\sum x}{n}$$ where $\sum x$ is the total and $n$ is the count.
It is the most common measure of central tendency.
[[imp:The mean is sensitive to extremely high or low values, which can distort it.]]

formulaCard.title: Weighted Mean and GPA
notes: Grade points: A = 4, B = 3, C = 2, D = 1, F = 0.
Weights are frequencies or credit hours.

explanation: The [[kw:weighted mean]] multiplies each value by its frequency (how many times it occurs) and then divides by the total of the frequencies.
Formula: $$\text{Weighted Mean} = \frac{\sum (\text{Value} \times \text{Frequency})}{\sum \text{Frequency}}$$
Your [[kw:grade point average (GPA)]] is a weighted mean: each grade point (A=4, B=3, etc.) is weighted by the number of credit hours.
$$\text{GPA} = \frac{\sum (\text{Grade Points} \times \text{Credits})}{\sum \text{Credits}}$$
[[imp:Weighted means are used when some data points are more important or occur more frequently.]]

blocks.title: 3. The Median

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: The median is not the same as the mean unless the data is perfectly symmetric. [[imp:In a symmetric distribution, mean = median.]]

visuals.title: Finding the Median (Odd Number of Values)
visuals.caption: With an even count, average the two middle values.

explanation: The [[kw:median]] is the middle value in an ordered list of numbers.
If the list has an odd number of values, the median is the middle one.
If the list has an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle values.
The median is not affected by extremely high or low values, making it a better measure for skewed data.
[[imp:Half the values are below the median and half are above.]]

formulaCard.title: Median Steps
notes: Use when the data has extreme values that distort the mean.
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Step 1: Order the values from smallest to largest.}$$ $$\text{Step 2: If odd count, middle value. If even count, average the two middle values.}$$

formulaCard.title: Mode Definition
notes: If two values tie for highest frequency, both are modes (bimodal).
If no value repeats, there is no mode.

explanation: The [[kw:mode]] is the value that occurs most often in a data set.
There can be one mode, more than one mode (bimodal, multimodal), or no mode if all values are different.
The mode is not affected by extreme values and can be used with non‑numeric data (e.g., most popular color).
[[imp:The mode shows the most frequent occurrence, not necessarily the center.]]

examples.prompt: Find the mode of the following test scores: 70, 85, 90, 85, 75, 70, 85.

The mode tells the most frequently sold size, so the manager knows which sizes to order most.

formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Mean: } \text{No extreme values, symmetric data.}$$ $$\text{Median: } \text{Data has outliers or is skewed.}$$ $$\text{Mode: } \text{Most common category or value needed.}$$
notes: Always compute all three to compare before deciding.

visuals.title: Blueprint: Which Measure to Use?

explanation: Apply the blueprint to descriptive statistics:
1. Understand: list all data values, note any extreme outliers, and determine what 'typical' means in context.
2. Solve: compute the mean, median, and mode. Compare them.
3. Conclude: choose the measure that best represents the data without distortion. For skewed data, median; for frequent values, mode; for symmetric, mean.
This systematic approach ensures you don't blindly use the mean when another measure is more appropriate.
